video_title: Linear vs. Exponential: AGI Has Arrived But Oil, Bonds and the Fed Oh My
gist: Jordi Visser argues investors are wasting attention on a 'linear' macro tape (oil, bond yields, Fed odds) while the week's actual news is that Jensen Huang declared AGI has arrived with OpenAI's Astra model, which ran 10,000 agents in parallel for 88 hours to crack Navier-Stokes. He builds the case that AI capex is rate-insensitive, that rising H100 rental prices (up 22% on the month) break the GPU-depreciation bear case and cut hyperscaler credit needs by hundreds of billions, that terminal-value compression makes multiple compression the dominant equity risk, and that Robinhood plus Ethereum are the entry point to the TradFi/AI/crypto convergence — with a DIY agentic trading-desk build as the actionable retail edge.

insights.claim: Visser dates the break between the 'linear' economy (driven by oil, bonds and rates) and the 'exponential' economy to 2008, attributing it to the iPhone's release the year before plus the growth of transfer payments and government debt, and says the MAG 7 was the trade that expressed it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frames any macro-first allocation process as structurally mispositioned; the implied portfolio tilt is toward exponential/tech exposure regardless of the rate cycle.
insights.quote: That all changed beginning in 2008. That is when the exponential world took off because of the release of iPhone the year before and because transfer payments started to grow

insights.claim: AI capex, not housing and autos, is now the marginal driver of the US economy, and Visser argues it is not rate-sensitive at all — which is why traditional rate-based economic forecasting fails.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If the economy's growth engine does not respond to the funds rate, Fed-path trades and rate-sensitive cyclicals lose their historical beta to the cycle.
insights.quote: AI capex is driving the economy. And as I showed last week, it is not at all rate sensitive.

insights.claim: Visser cites a week in which core CPI and PPI both came in hotter than expected, Fed odds shifted, crude rallied and the war worsened — yet the S&P 500 was up slightly over the two days — as direct evidence that the classic macro inputs no longer move equities.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A live falsification test for macro-driven positioning: when bad macro prints produce no equity damage, the market is telling you the driver has changed.
insights.quote: on a day where we had higher than expected core inflation yesterday, we had higher than expected PPI, the probability the Fed went up, crude oil went through, the war is getting worse, and over the two days... the S&P was up slightly

insights.claim: Visser argues GDP is the wrong instrument for measuring the current productivity boom because it is a 1930s industrial-production index that does not count IP, so the acceleration in productivity is showing up in profit margins rather than in official statistics.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Suggests watching corporate margin series rather than BLS/BEA productivity prints to time the AI productivity trade, and discounting economists who say productivity has not risen.
insights.quote: The model of GDP is wrong. You can't say that GDP, the index created in the 1930s to measure industrial production, is the right metric to be using to say productivity is not higher.

insights.claim: Visser recommends reading Anthropic's in-house economics team over Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley economics because sell-side economists do not know which models are coming and therefore forecast linearly.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An information-sourcing edge: lab-affiliated economists have forward visibility on model capability that sell-side rate forecasts structurally lack.
insights.quote: Most economists have no idea what models are coming up. The anthropicus economists do.

insights.claim: Visser uses HYG relative to IEF as his real-time equity-risk overlay instead of quoted credit spreads, and notes that in the latest week HYG rose relative to IEF — high yield held in while Treasuries sold off — confirming the equity rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A liquid, intraday-observable credit proxy for equity risk that flagged the 2022 drawdown; a rollover in HYG/IEF would be the first sign the AI bid is breaking.
insights.quote: HYG relative to IEF, the proxy that I'll use real time and the one that I care the most about as an overlay rel instead of spreads.

insights.claim: Bond volatility, junk spreads and TIPS-implied inflation expectations are all failing to move despite hot inflation prints and rising Fed hike odds, which Visser reads as the market signalling indifference to the macro headlines.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cross-asset confirmation to fade macro-headline-driven equity de-risking until credit or vol actually breaks.
insights.quote: bond va's not moving, junk spreads aren't moving. Uh any part the inflation expectations via tips not moving like the market is saying h we don't really care about what's going on.

insights.claim: Earnings revisions are still rising (32 up on the week on a 20-week average basis) and PMI-based leading indicators are strong, which Visser uses to rebut the 'peak earnings' objection to high valuations.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Revisions turning down — not the Fed — would be the actual sell signal for the AI complex.

insights.claim: Visser says the S&P 500's PEG ratio is the cheapest it has been in at least 30 years, and that with revisions still rising and profit margins not yet rolling over, the 'peak earnings' bear case has no confirmation.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes an apparently expensive index as cheap on growth-adjusted terms; margins rolling over is the specific trigger to watch, since it historically leads revisions.
insights.quote: the market has never been cheaper or at least in the last 30 plus years with the PEG ratio down here

insights.claim: Visser reads the S&P 500 as holding its 50-day moving average in a flag formation after a high, barely up since June 2nd, and argues this sideways consolidation can persist indefinitely unless earnings actually roll over.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sets the base case as range/consolidation rather than top, with earnings — not price action — as the arbiter.
insights.quote: unless the economy is going to fall off and earnings are going to fall off, as far as I'm concerned, we can keep doing this for a while

insights.claim: Visser describes Treasury Secretary Bessent's upsized buybacks (to six billion) being immediately sold, and floats that the administration's 'plan B' is to cut long-term issuance outright if the buyback push fails to contain long yields.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit policy path for suppressing the long end; duration traders should price the risk that supply, not demand, is the swing variable.
insights.quote: Is it talk time to talk about plan B? If this doesn't work, they'll just cut long-term issuance outright.

insights.claim: Visser frames the bond market as openly daring the incoming Fed leadership, noting Fed rate-hike odds surged to 90% while Bessent and Warsh — both installed by the Trump administration, which does not want higher rates — publicly fight market participants.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fighting a government with both a third mandate on long-term rates and issuance control has historically been a losing trade; Visser's conclusion is to avoid the fight rather than buy bonds.
insights.quote: the market is testing you, Warsh. This is a double dog daring you. This is straight schoolyard.

themes.theme: AGI Arrival: Astra and Agent Swarms

insights.claim: Jensen Huang declared that AGI has arrived with OpenAI's Astra model, which Visser says should have been the week's dominant news story rather than a 10bp move in bond yields.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If a credible capability threshold has been crossed, positioning against the AI complex is fighting a step-change, not a cycle.
insights.quote: Jensen Yuang, the godfather of AI, said AGI has arrived with Astra.

insights.claim: Astra was trained on roughly 100,000 GPUs, the next model is four times that size, and the Vera Rubin generation sits behind that — a compute escalation Visser uses to argue against fading the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A visible multi-generation compute pipeline underwrites the capex forecast that AI-infrastructure equities are discounting.
insights.quote: 100,000k is what basically Astro was trained on. The next model is four times the size and behind that the Vera Rubins. Why fade this guys?

insights.claim: Research agents are reportedly generating 3.1 workdays of output for every human workday, and 10,000 AI agents working in parallel for 88 hours hit the Navier-Stokes challenge that mathematicians have pursued for decades.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, quantified productivity multiple for digital labor — the input that drives the margin-expansion thesis rather than a headcount-reduction story.
insights.quote: research agents are now generating 3.1 workdays for every human workday

insights.claim: Visser's causal chain is that compute converts into intelligence, intelligence multiplies into thousands of parallel agents, and those agents get pointed at foundational science problems — meaning compute demand scales with the number of problems worth solving, not with headcount.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Implies GPU demand is far more elastic and durable than a software-adoption S-curve would suggest, supporting sustained pricing power in compute.
insights.quote: Compute can increasingly be converted into intelligence. Intelligence can be multiplied into thousands of agents.

insights.claim: Visser replaces the classic growth formula (more people plus more capital plus higher productivity) with a model where digital labor substitutes for population growth, arguing the binding constraint on GDP shifts from human headcount to compute, energy and deployment capacity.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reorients long-horizon growth exposure toward compute and power supply chains and away from demographic-driven growth assumptions.
insights.quote: The old constraint on GDP was ultimately the number of humans and the productivity of their time. The new constraint may increasingly become compute, energy, and our ability to deploy intelligence.

insights.claim: Visser argues the agent productivity gap is structural rather than marginal because agents have no lunch breaks, smoking breaks, daydreaming or emotions, and estimates they work at three to five times human effective output.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Supports the view that margin expansion, not revenue growth, will be the dominant earnings driver for AI adopters.

insights.claim: OpenAI is converging chat, agents, desktop, Codex, tools and image models into one surface, which Visser says is the inflection point that makes agent use accessible to mainstream knowledge workers rather than only to developers.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Product consolidation, not raw capability, is the variable that converts model progress into measurable enterprise and consumer adoption.

insights.claim: Demand for Astra is outrunning capacity — Visser cites 6.2 million views and says OpenAI is already running out of space for it, alongside Microsoft's plan to triple its data center computing power and its reiterated capacity shortage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capacity shortage at the largest hyperscaler is the cleanest confirmation that the capex cycle has not peaked.
insights.quote: Demand for Astra is really unprecedented. 6.2 million views. They're running out of space for it already.

insights.claim: H100 rental prices are roughly unchanged from three years ago and rose 22% over the past month, versus a normal chip-aging path that Visser says would have implied a 40-50% decline — directly falsifying the depreciation-fraud bear case made by Michael Burry and Jim Chanos.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The single most checkable datapoint in the AI-accounting debate; a sustained rollover in rental rates would revive the short thesis, while continued strength invalidates it.
insights.quote: H100 rental prices are almost at the same level as they were three years ago. Think about that, guys. They're at the same price.

insights.claim: Visser echoes Gavin Baker's point from a month earlier that the market assumed GPU rental prices would steadily fall, while older GPUs are in fact holding value and in some cases repricing higher — which changes the hyperscaler financing debate.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A named, dated call that has since been confirmed by the tape — worth tracking as a leading indicator for hyperscaler cash-flow revisions.
insights.quote: His core point was that the market was assuming GPU rental prices would steadily fall... Instead, older GPUs were holding their value far better than expected.

insights.claim: Because hyperscalers can reprice existing compute upward when contracts roll — Visser's analogy is buying tomatoes at $2 and selling at $20 — cloud cash-flow estimates are far too low and the sector may need hundreds of billions less credit than expected.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Second-order trade: if AI-related debt issuance shrinks rather than balloons, the AI-credit-bubble short and the associated spread widening both fail.
insights.quote: This could remove hundreds of billions of dollars of expected credit needs.

insights.claim: Visser's core framing of the debate is that accounting depreciation schedules and the actual rental market now disagree about GPU economics, and the rental market is the one with real transactions behind it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Gives a falsifiable test for both sides of the Nvidia/hyperscaler debate rather than a narrative argument.
insights.quote: whether or not you agree with it, the market is depreciating GPUs, the rental market is not, that's the issue

insights.claim: Visser notes Paul Tudor Jones published a negative piece on AI that is about the financial trade rather than the technology, and says the two have exchanged emails — framing the bear case as genuine engagement rather than ignorance.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Flags that credible macro capital is positioned skeptically on the AI trade, which is itself information about crowding.

themes.theme: Terminal Value Compression and the Entrepreneurship Hedge

insights.claim: Visser's central valuation framework is that AI simultaneously expands the total addressable economy through scientific breakthroughs while shortening corporate duration, so total-market TAM rises even as individual companies' terminal values and multiples compress.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains how an index can be cheap on PEG while individual multiples de-rate — argues for owning the beneficiaries of TAM expansion rather than incumbents with long-duration earnings assumptions.
insights.quote: we get to a point where the TAM gets bigger at the same time that corporate duration gets shorter

insights.claim: Visser says multiple compression has already happened in software and is now happening in hardware, citing Nvidia trading at what he calls a cheap PE, and argues the open question is what multiple a disrupted, non-growing company deserves.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Warns that cheap optical PEs in AI hardware are the market pricing shortened duration, not a valuation opportunity — screen on growth persistence rather than multiple.
insights.quote: Multiples are going to compress because terminal value, the ability to know when a company will have a cliff of their earnings no longer growing.

insights.claim: Visser explicitly caps expectations for AI hardware winners: he does not expect Micron to repeat its prior twelve-bagger, sees roughly $1,600-$2,000 as a realistic range from about $1,000, and says most days the names will be flat or down with the entire annual return concentrated in about 5% of days.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Directly argues against buy-and-hold in the AI leaders and for a momentum/entry-timing overlay — missing roughly five days means missing the whole move.
insights.quote: at the end of the year, maybe 5% of the rally, the days will be the rallies you need to miss. And if you miss those five days, you miss the whole move.

insights.claim: Visser argues most layoffs ahead will not come from thriving AI-enabled firms but from companies under competitive pressure because AI can now do what they do — making employment at an incumbent a riskier position than entrepreneurship.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Shortened moat duration is both an equity-selection filter and a personal-capital allocation argument; distinguishes 'AI efficiency' layoffs from 'AI disruption' layoffs.
insights.quote: They need to fire people because they're under pressure. And they're under pressure because AI can do these things all the time.

insights.claim: Visser relays Sundar Pichai's warning that failing to learn agent orchestration now means spending 2027 catching up to those who started today, and endorses it as literally true.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete 12-18 month window in which agent-orchestration skill becomes the differentiating human capital in knowledge work.
insights.quote: if you don't learn how to orchestrate agents now, you'll spend 2027 catching up to people who started today

insights.claim: Visser reports running six AI agents (including ones named Probe and Prism) on a trading account via Astra, turning $500 into $5,100 by morning, while explicitly dismissing the P&L as meaningless — the point is the agent architecture, not the backtest result.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A working demonstration that retail-accessible agents can run a research-to-execution loop; the capability, not the return, is the tradable signal.
insights.quote: I could care less about these back tests and people making money. I don't care.

insights.claim: Visser's design principle for an AI trading desk is aggressive rejection: thousands of ideas generated daily, roughly 99% rejected at the first filter and 90% of survivors rejected at the next, mirroring how a multi-strategy fund like Millennium allocates.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes AI's edge in quant research as search-and-filter capacity rather than prediction — the value is in the rejection rate, not the idea generation.
insights.quote: The great thing about a back test is it should fail most of the time. And to build an AI trading desk, the system is designed to reject almost everything.

insights.claim: Visser argues retail investors can build a mini multi-strategy fund by running ten uncorrelated agent-driven strategies with $50-$100 each, and that agents will outperform humans on the execution side specifically because they have no emotions.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Democratization of multi-strat construction pressures the fee structure of small-capacity systematic managers while expanding brokerage engagement per user.

insights.claim: Visser built a technical entry system for his 100-name AI thematic universe around a structural-trend / reset / coiled / ignition sequence using average true range and rate of change, based on his view that market structure now makes investors late to moves and forces earlier exits.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable entry/exit overlay for a structural bull market where the buy-and-hold path is punishing; he cites it as how he exited Micron well before the top.
insights.quote: I'm looking for structural bull markets. When things get overdone, I want to basically be out based on rate of change and then I want to wait for them to reset.

insights.claim: Visser says momentum becomes the dominant factor at exponential inflection points because the experience of the past ten years is less useful for responding today.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues for factor rotation into momentum and against mean-reversion/value frameworks calibrated on the post-GFC regime.
insights.quote: That's why I think momentum becomes a dominant factor

insights.claim: Over 80% of the names in Visser's 100-stock AI universe are above an upward-sloping 200-day moving average, which he treats as confirmation of a structural bull market in the AI capex complex rather than a narrow rally.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Breadth within the theme is the health check; a drop below this threshold would signal the capex trade narrowing to a handful of names.

insights.claim: Robinhood, Moomoo and Interactive Brokers have all shipped agentic investing capability — Moomoo since April 23rd with paper trading, APIs and proprietary price data that Visser says is better than Yahoo Finance — making retail agent deployment an infrastructure reality as of June 2026.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Brokerages competing on agent APIs and data quality is a new differentiation axis that should drive engagement, order flow and account acquisition.

insights.claim: Visser calls Robinhood the epicenter of the AI-crypto-macro nexus — a trading company that is under-monetizing crypto relative to its other businesses and is simultaneously an agentic company — and says it is the best single entry point for understanding the convergence from an earnings perspective.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A single listed vehicle expressing three converging themes; the under-monetized crypto segment is the optionality.
insights.quote: Robin Hood is basically the epicenter of AI crypto macro nexus.

insights.claim: Robinhood Chain has been live only two months and is already generating a record $6 million in daily fees, with Bernstein seeing 31% upside on the stock as its chain fees top Solana's.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Onchain fee revenue is becoming a reportable earnings line for a listed brokerage — a new, fast-compounding revenue stream TradFi research has barely modeled.
insights.quote: Robin Hood chain has only been live for two months and it's already starting to rerate the onchain market.

insights.claim: Visser points out that Arbitrum surged 7.87% on Robinhood Chain news while a Wall Street Journal search for Arbitrum returned no results — arguing the information gap between crypto-native and traditional financial media is itself the alpha source.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Price-moving catalysts in the onchain layer are not covered by TradFi media, creating a tractable and repeatable information edge.
insights.quote: Arbitron Wall Street Journal did not match any news results. Shocking.

insights.claim: Robinhood's five takeaways from the Goldman Sachs technology conference were that agentic trading is going mainstream, the chain is global financial infrastructure, it wants the entire financial relationship (trading, crypto, retirement, banking), prediction markets are a gateway product, and it is becoming an AI-native tokenized platform — which Visser likens to Apple.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Platform expansion into banking and retirement changes Robinhood's comparable set and TAM from brokerage to full financial platform.
insights.quote: a hedge fund in your pocket

insights.claim: Visser argues getting into tokenization ahead of TradFi is the trade because institutions will be forced in to generate alpha, and the Clarity Act is the catalyst — though he puts the probability of passage this year at below 20% even as Coinbase's Brian Armstrong and Patrick Witt say it is ready for a yes vote.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Asymmetric setup: low odds of near-term passage but large institutional-credibility unlock if it happens; positions ahead of pension and institutional flows.
insights.quote: The probabilities for this year of getting it through are still below 20%. But that doesn't mean they can't get a yes vote.

insights.claim: Visser stacks the week's institutional tokenization signals — NASDAQ investing $100 million in Kraken targeting a 2027 tokenized stock launch, US banks testing stablecoins, Visa's stablecoin card business exploding, and European banks planning a euro stablecoin on Ethereum — as evidence that incumbents are already preparing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Institutional infrastructure buildout is pre-positioning for tokenized securities well before the regulatory framework lands.

themes.theme: Valuing Ethereum and the AI Trust Premium

insights.claim: Visser believes Ethereum should outperform Bitcoin in a genuine bull market because of its ecosystem and network effects on the agentic side, and notes ETH broke out against BTC to its highest level since January.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A specific relative-value expression (ETH/BTC ratio) tied to the agentic thesis rather than to generic crypto beta.
insights.quote: I think Ethereum should be outperforming Bitcoin when we're actually in the bull market

insights.claim: Visser argues William Mougayar's decade-old TED talk on Ethereum scored roughly 8/10 on direction but 5/10 on specifics — he was too aggressive on removing intermediaries (Robinhood is the counterexample), missed stablecoins entirely, and most importantly missed AI agents, which may be what finally makes his thesis work.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The original disintermediation thesis failed because it assumed human users; agent-to-agent transactions are the missing demand driver that revalues the base layer.
insights.quote: The biggest thing he didn't see was AI agents and this ironically they may finally make his thesis work.

insights.claim: Visser applies the internet-valuation history to crypto: the market priced eyeballs first, then revenue, then SaaS metrics roughly 25 years later — so crypto's valuation metrics (revenue, network effects, money flow, ecosystem value, productive assets, programmability) are still being invented.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Argues that the absence of an accepted valuation model is a feature of the early phase, not evidence of no value — the metric gap is where the mispricing lives.

insights.claim: Visser draws a direct analogy between Ethereum and Amazon: Amazon ran +27,000% from its 1997 bookstore days to 2013 while never having a PE below 100 until 2017-2018, and Ethereum is up roughly 3,000% from its lows — implying the bulk of the move happens before a valuation framework exists.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The explicit warning to institutional allocators: waiting for a defensible valuation model is how you miss the move, as he personally did with Amazon.
insights.quote: when you're trying to figure out how to value crypto by the time it gets to the point where it's no longer a ridiculous price, you've already lost 27,000%

insights.claim: Visser argues AI turns trust into a priced economic asset and that Ethereum is the trust model, concluding that real-world assets will have to move onchain for the blockchain to retain value.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Positions RWA tokenization as necessary rather than optional, and frames Ethereum's moat as verification rather than throughput.
insights.quote: AI makes trust an economic asset. I'm 100% sure that the blockchain needs every real world asset to go on there to keep its value.

insights.claim: Visser links escalating AI-enabled cyberattacks — Iranian hackers shutting a UK power plant, Boston Scientific and Stryker falling on cyberattack fallout with Boston Scientific cutting its earnings forecast, and Anthropic disclosing a fourth AI hacking incident involving Opus 4.6 plus Iranian targeting of US Navy warships — to his bullishness on crypto, because AI destroys trust in everything.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cyber risk is now an earnings-guidance event, and Visser's second-order read is that it accrues to verifiable-trust infrastructure while hurting small companies that cannot defend themselves.
insights.quote: I think AI leads to not trusting anything and it will not stop the earnings. It will not stock productivity, but it will hurt smaller businesses and smaller companies that can't protect themselves.

insights.claim: Visser reports that the wallet and application layer on top of crypto is where hackings are actually occurring, not the chain itself — a distinction he says matters for how investors underwrite crypto security risk.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Separates base-layer risk from app-layer risk, which argues for differentiating custody and application exposure within a crypto allocation.
insights.quote: the chain is safe but the apps that are on top for everything have become an issue
